beats.gist: Off Horta, the guide explains that today's task is to come up quietly behind a whale under sail, and Manuel asks the crew to set the sail neither too tight nor too loose.
The whale has seen the boat and dived, so Manuel tells the crew to ease the sheets and slow down.
Once the boat has slowed, Manuel tells the young crew member, without any lecture, that you wait and do not chase. This is a pure character line with no factual claim about whale behaviour.
The sail is flapping, so Manuel gives a short order to bear away.
The young crew member asks what the flapping was. Manuel names it 'panejar' and says it comes from easing too much or pointing too close to the wind, and that a noisy sail is not a quiet approach.

beats.concept: Fine trim on a steady heading
beats.gist: On the slow stretch, Manuel and the young crew member talk quietly about keeping the sail just right: too loose deflects less air, too tight breaks the airflow. Lines play one after another as a pool.

Close astern of the whale, Manuel says nothing for a moment, then gives one short, plain line acknowledging what boats like this were once used for, with no glory or detail. Until a source is supplied, he uses a generic, fact-free line instead.

The guide closes by saying the group watched the whale, they did not hunt it. Manuel's last word is about the boat, not the whale, and the visitors turn back for Horta. There is no score for the approach.
An optional 'what is real' card: the guide, Manuel and the crew member are invented, while the sailing terms used on board (sail trim, panejar) come from sources.

evidence.text: Caravels from Galicia sailed to Cabo Branco to fish sharks and mullets, which were dried in the sun like cod from Newfoundland. · who: Galician caravel crews · place: Cabo Branco · when: 1582 · cargo: chiens de mer (sharks), mullets, other fish
High-sea fishing beyond the bar: “alto” (pt-PT) — High sea; in Lisbon of that era, fishing 'do alto' meant fishing beyond the river bar, not at a set distance from the coast.
High-sea fishing beyond the bar: “barra” (pt-PT) — The bar or entrance of the Tagus at Lisbon, where fishing outside it was authorised and pilots worked.
Coastal navigation: “navegação costeira” (pt-PT) — Coastal navigation, such as trips to the Algarve to fetch produce or trade with Moroccan ports.
Sail trim: “Trim (ease or sheet in)” (en) — Matching the sail setting to the heading; a marker turns green when correct.

numbers: wind angle in over-sheeted example (beam wind): 90 degrees
evidence.text: Sail trim: “Ajuste das Velas” (pt-BR) — Sail trim: sails should be neither over-sheeted nor over-eased; too loose deflects less air, too tight breaks the airflow.
Luffing (sail flapping): “Panejar” (pt-BR) — Luffing: the sail flapping irregularly, from over-easing the sheet or pointing closer to the wind than close-hauled.
Caravel (lateen-rigged): “caravela” () — Lateen-rigged vessel that was adapted and improved for difficult long-distance Discovery voyages.
Preserved fish cargo: “peixe fumado ou salgado” () — Smoked or salted fish, a preserved cargo shipped to Castile, Aragon, Italy, England, Flanders and other regions.
Preserved fish cargo: “salgado e curado” () — Fish preserved by salting and curing, kept in fishermen's houses and sold alongside fresh fish.
